app.tagline: set the toss, footwork and swing, and watch whether the ball clears the net.

winner.title: return error
winner.sub: there's a good chance they hit it, but it doesn't clear the net or goes out

tough.title: tough return
tough.sub: it comes back, but under pressure

easy.title: easy return
easy.sub: they had time to set up and swing

reason.heat: faster than they are used to

tips.lowToss: toss higher so you can hit it at full reach, or jump higher.
tips.net: toss a little further back, brush up for more topspin, or hit lower on the ball.
tips.longAuto: toss a little further in front, or brush up for more topspin to bring it down.
tips.longManual: angle the racket down a touch, or brush up for more topspin.
tips.wide: aim a bit more inside the box.

risk.label: Error tolerance
risk.sub: land in when hit with small mistakes
risk.window: the racket angle can be off by {{down}}° before it hits the net, or +{{up}}° before it goes long.
risk.misses: even hit perfectly, this serve misses. change something to bring it in.
risk.against: against a {{level}} returner: {{won}}% of points won outright, {{fault}}% faults.
risk.method: from {{tries}} tries at this serve, each a little off: about ±{{angle}}° racket angle, ±{{yaw}}° aim, ±{{speed}}% speed, ±{{rpm}}% spin and ±{{brush}}° in brush direction. that last one is why slice is riskier: with the spin tipped sideways, a slightly different brush changes how much the ball dips. a return error means they likely hit it, but into the net or out. an easy return means they have time to set up and swing.
risk.insideOut: this one goes out toward your hitting-arm side, so you hold back your shoulder turn and steer with the arm: your aim wanders about ±{{yaw}}° instead of ±{{base}}°.
risk.acrossBody: this one goes across your body, with your natural swing, so it's easy to repeat.

target.drag: or drag on the court map.
target.beginner: a beginner: slow to react and uneasy with pace, so most serves win the point.
target.club: a club player: handles a steady serve, but pace, width or a big kick cause trouble.
target.strong: a strong club player: quick to react, so serves need pace and placement.
target.advanced: an advanced player: fast hands and feet. you need a big, well-placed serve, or a kick or slice that pulls them off the court.
target.deuceNote: serving from right of the centre mark into the box on your left.
target.adNote: serving from left of the centre mark into the box on your right.

toss.title: Toss
toss.peaksBelow: peaks at {{apex}}, below your {{reach}} reach, so you hit it lower.
toss.peaks: peaks {{apex}} off the ground and rises with your height and jump. in the air for {{t}} s.
toss.padLabel: toss placement: arrow keys move it forward, back and sideways

server.title: Server
server.mirror: switching mirrors your toss, brush and contact point, so it's the same serve played the other way.
server.heightHint: a taller server reaches higher: you meet the ball at {{h}}.
server.platformNote: feet stay apart the whole time, and you meet the ball right where you tossed it. steady and simple.
server.pinpointNote: the back foot slides up beside the front foot, then both drive up and into the court: you meet the ball {{forward}} further in and {{lift}} higher, and land inside the baseline.
server.jumpHint: jumping higher meets the ball higher, which gives more room over the net.

swing.title: Swing and spin
swing.lede: How hard you hit, how your racket brushes the ball, and where on the ball you make contact.
swing.speedHint: a faster ball has less time to drop, so it needs more spin to land in.
swing.upHint: swinging up the back of the ball adds topspin, which pulls it down into the box.
swing.acrossHintRighty: brushing across to the right adds slice, which curves the ball left.
swing.acrossHintLefty: brushing across to the left adds slice, which curves the ball right.
swing.contactHintRighty: low on the ball adds topspin and sends it up. the right side (3 o'clock) adds slice and pushes it left. high on the ball flattens it out and drives it down.
swing.contactHintLefty: low on the ball adds topspin and sends it up. the left side (9 o'clock) adds slice and pushes it right. high on the ball flattens it out and drives it down.

notes.flat: almost no spin: the ball flies straight and fast, with little room over the net.
notes.topspin: the ball dips down into the box, so it can cross the net higher.
notes.kick: heavy topspin: a big dip, then a high bounce.
notes.topspin-slice_right: dips and curves a little to the left.
notes.topspin-slice_left: dips and curves a little to the right.
notes.slice_right: mostly side spin: curves left and stays low after the bounce.
notes.slice_left: mostly side spin: curves right and stays low after the bounce.
notes.reverse_right: side spin the other way: curves right.
notes.reverse_left: side spin the other way: curves left.

racket.title: Racket angle
racket.auto: auto: the server angles the racket to land in the box, as if the toss were perfect
racket.hint: negative closes the face and drives the ball down. a toss in front tilts it down, behind tilts it up. the racket in the animation tilts to match at contact.

ball.side: {{clock}} o'clock, the side of the ball
ball.caption: hitting at {{where}}. the arrow is your brush.
ball.label: contact point on the ball: arrow keys move it

map.label: court from above; drag to aim

compare.colors: line color for the new serve

recommend.title: Recommended serves
recommend.for: for a {{height}} {{hand}} server on the {{side}} side, against a {{level}} returner. change any of these and the picks update.
recommend.maxSpeedHint: your fastest flat serve. spin takes some of that pace: a kick comes off about a quarter slower.

why.first: worth a risk: when it misses you still get a second serve.
why.second: goes in at least {{floor}}% of the time, since a double fault loses the point. of those, it's the one that wins the most.

recommend.insideOut: it goes out to your hitting-arm side, which is harder to control.
recommend.acrossBody: it goes across your body, with your natural swing.
recommend.total: together you'd win about {{won}}% of your service points, with {{df}}% double faults.
recommend.method: found by trying {{n}} serves (four spins, six directions, five speeds) with your height, hand, stance and jump, using the same physics and error tolerance as above. after a tough return the server is assumed to win {{tough}}% of rallies, after an easy one {{easy}}%. a rough guide, not a rule.

simple.title: Simple mode
simple.lede: Tap where you want your serve to land and pick a serve: flat, slice, topspin-slice or kick. You'll see the speed and spin that get it there best, how much room for error it has, how hard it is to return, and how it scores.
simple.courtLabel: the service box seen from behind you: tap or drag to place the ball, arrow keys move it
simple.spotFacts: {{deep}} inside the service line, {{across}} inside the {{line}}
simple.courtHint: the shaded oval is where 9 in 10 of the chosen serve land: the more of it past a line, the less margin. tap the other box to serve from the other side.
simple.speedHint: your fastest flat serve. spin takes some of that pace.
simple.backToPick: back to the recommended speed and spin

why.safest: of the ways to hit this serve there, the one that lands in most.
why.hardest: of the ways to hit this serve there that land in often enough, the hardest to return.
why.both: of the ways to hit this serve there, the one that lands in most, and the hardest to return.
why.balance: the best mix of landing in and pressure on the returner.

simple.aimRight: aim about {{d}} right of the spot: the spin bends it back
simple.aimLeft: aim about {{d}} left of the spot: the spin bends it back
simple.options: Best ways to hit this {{spin}} serve
simple.cantSpin: a {{spin}} serve can't land there. try another spot or another serve.
simple.warnFirst: this spot is hard to hit with this serve: even the best speed and spin land in only {{p}}% of the time. try a spot deeper in the box or further from the lines, or another serve.
simple.warnSecond: this serve doesn't land here 9 times in 10 at any speed or spin, so it's risky for a second serve. try a spot further from the lines, or another serve.
simple.method: the tool tries the serve you picked with a lighter and a heavier brush, at several speeds up to the fastest it can be hit, finds the racket angle and aim that land each one on your spot, and flies each with the same small mistakes as the full tool. the score is the points you'd win out of 100 serves like it: aces and return errors win, and after a return you win {{tough}}% of rallies after a tough one and {{easy}}% after an easy one. the recommended one scores best of those that land in often enough (at least half the time for a first serve, 9 times in 10 for a second); if none do, it's the one that lands in most. on a first serve a miss goes to your second serve (your {{second}} to the same spot, which wins about {{secondWins}}%), so it can take more risk.

game.title: Play a game
game.note: you serve every point to your spot with the serves you picked, against the returner set above. a fault gives you a second serve.
game.stats: points won {{won}} of {{points}} · aces {{aces}} · double faults {{doubles}} · first serves in {{first}}%

result.winner: Return error: they got a racket on it but couldn't keep it in. Point to you.
result.toughWon: Tough return, and you won the rally.
result.toughLost: Tough return, but they won the rally.
result.easyWon: Easy return, but you still won the rally.
result.easyLost: Easy return, and they won the rally.

seo.title: Serve Visualization Tool: free 3D tennis serve simulator
seo.description: A free 3D tennis serve simulator. Adjust your toss, stance, jump, swing, spin and speed, watch whether the ball clears the net, and see your error tolerance and your chances of an ace against returners from NTRP 2.0 to 5.0.
seo.simpleTitle: Simple mode: tap a spot, pick a serve, get the best speed and spin | Serve Visualization Tool
seo.simpleDescription: Tap where you want your tennis serve to land, pick flat, slice, topspin-slice or kick, and see the speed and spin that get it there best, with its margin for error, how hard it is to return and a score. Then play a practice game against a returner from NTRP 2.0 to 5.0.
seo.aboutTitle: How the Serve Visualization Tool works: the tennis serve math, explained simply
seo.aboutDescription: How the free Serve Visualization Tool models a tennis serve: ball flight, spin, the bounce, the toss, error tolerance and the returner, explained in plain words with the formulas behind them.
seo.noscript: This interactive 3D tool needs JavaScript turned on.

about.title: About the Serve Visualization Tool
about.intro: I made this free tool to help me and my friends work on our serves: to see how the toss, footwork and swing change where the ball goes, and how hard it is to return. It stays free to use, but keeping it online costs money every year for the domain name and the cloud hosting. If you can and like the tool, chipping in on PayPal helps cover those costs and keeps it running.

flight.title: 1. How the ball flies
flight.body: The ball is moved forward in tiny steps, 1,000 times a second. At each step three things act on it: gravity pulls it down, air drag slows it, and spin pushes it down or sideways. Add them up, update the speed, update the position, and repeat.
flight.note: gravity is 9.81 m/s² straight down. drag grows with the square of the speed, so a 200 km/h serve feels four times the drag of a 100 km/h one.

spin.title: 2. Why spin bends the ball
spin.body: A spinning ball drags the air around with it. Topspin throws air up behind the ball, so the ball is pushed down: it dips into the box, which lets you hit higher over the net. Side spin pushes the ball sideways, which is why a slice curves.
spin.note: v is the ball's speed, r its radius and ω how fast it spins. more spin, or a slower ball, means a stronger push.

bounce.title: 3. The bounce
bounce.body: When the ball lands it keeps about 75% of its downward speed, now going up. Friction with the court slows it and pulls its spin toward rolling. A ball that comes in low and fast skids through instead, so a flat serve keeps more of its pace. Heavy topspin grips the court and kicks the ball up higher: that is the kick serve.
bounce.formula: speed up after = 0.75 × speed down before + kick
bounce.note: the kick is a small extra push that grows with topspin.

toss.title: 4. The toss and where you hit the ball
toss.body: Your reach is how high the racket can meet the ball: your height, your arm and racket, plus your jump. The toss height is measured above that reach, so taller players and bigger jumps toss higher. A toss that peaks below your reach forces a lower contact. A toss in front tilts the racket down; one behind tilts it up.
toss.formula: time in the air = √(2 × rise ÷ g) + √(2 × fall ÷ g)
toss.note: rise is how far the ball climbs after it leaves your hand, fall is how far it drops back to where you hit it, and g is gravity.

swing.title: 5. Spin from your swing
swing.body: Brushing up the back of the ball makes topspin; brushing across it makes side spin. Where you hit the ball adds to the brush: low on the ball adds topspin, the outside adds slice. The two parts combine like the sides of a right triangle.
swing.note: for example, 1,800 rpm of topspin and 3,200 rpm of side spin make about 3,650 rpm in total.

tolerance.title: 6. Error tolerance
tolerance.body: Nobody hits the same serve twice. The tool flies your serve again with each kind of small mistake on its own (racket angle, aim, speed, spin and brush direction), measures how far each one moves the ball, then adds those effects up over 1,024 evenly spread tries. The share that still lands in the box is your error tolerance.
tolerance.formula: error tolerance = tries that land in ÷ all tries
tolerance.note: slice is riskier because a slightly different brush changes how much topspin is left to bring the ball down.

returner.title: 7. The returner
returner.body: The returner waits just behind the baseline, about a metre inside the singles sideline. The tool works out when the ball reaches them and how far they have to move. They wait out their reaction time, then run, and can reach further still with a lunge, their arm and the racket. A ball coming toward them they meet at their usual spot; one curving away from them they cut off, moving diagonally forward to meet it earlier on its path, at the nearest point they can still reach in time. If there is no such point, it is an ace. Otherwise less time, a longer run or a lunge, more pace, a high kick or a low slice all make the return harder, from an easy return to a return error. A high kick is mostly trouble on the backhand (the returner is right-handed), and only when it comes too quickly for them to step back or move in. Their level sets all of it: how quickly they react and run, how far they lunge, how far forward they dare to cut off a wide ball, how fast a serve they're used to, and how often they miss even an easy one.
returner.formula: can reach = lunge, arm and racket + distance run after reacting
returner.note: a 2.0 returner reacts in about 0.42 s, runs about 3 m/s, reaches about 1.35 m, is used to serves up to about 85 km/h and misses about 1 easy return in 7; a 5.0 returner reacts in about 0.25 s, runs about 5 m/s, reaches about 1.8 m, is used to serves up to about 175 km/h and misses about 1 in 50.

direction.title: 8. Court side and your hitting arm
direction.body: The ad court isn't just the deuce court flipped. Your arm swings up and across your body, so a serve sent that way (a right-hander's slice out wide on the deuce side) goes with the swing. A serve sent out to your hitting-arm side (a right-hander's serve on the ad side) is hit inside-out: you hold back the shoulder turn and steer with the arm, so the aim, racket angle and pace wander more. A kick relies less on the turn, so it pays less. For a left-hander it's all the other way round, which is why their slice out wide on the ad side is such a weapon.
direction.formula: extra error = 4% per degree inside-out + 0.8% per degree across, less for a swing that brushes up
direction.note: the aim wanders by the full amount, the racket angle by half and the pace by about a third.

recommend.title: 9. Recommended serves
recommend.body: Give your height, hand and fastest serve, and the tool tries 120 serves: four spins, six directions and five speeds, each flown with the same small mistakes as the error tolerance. Spin costs pace: a kick comes off about a quarter slower than your fastest flat serve. The second serve has to go in at least 9 times in 10; of those it picks the one that wins the most points. The first serve can take more risk, because a miss only costs you the gap to your second serve.
recommend.formula: first serve value = in% × points won when in + (1 − in%) × second serve value
recommend.note: points won after a return are rough guesses: 58% after a tough return, 42% after an easy one.

limits.title: 10. Good to know
limits.body: The physics is meant to be believable, not exact. Drag and lift use typical textbook values, and the toss, jump, brush and returner are simple models of what coaches describe, not measured data. Use it to build intuition, then check it on court.
